title: recovery-choreography-and-terraform-hooks-dry-run-notes
body:
Purpose:
This is a working note capturing a lightweight recovery choreography for Private Deployments (VPC / on-prem) with emphasis on terraform hooks, state handling, and a reproducible dry-run checklist. The goal is to have an operator-friendly sequence that:
  - Minimizes blast radius during restoration
  - Keeps terraform state consistent across restore and upgrade windows
  - Provides fast smoke checks to verify service-level readiness
  - Documents fallbacks/rollback for in-place upgrades

Scope and assumptions:
  - Applies to Private Deployments (customer-managed control plane + on-prem inference nodes).
  - Object store: S3-compatible (MinIO or S3) for snapshots and artifacts.
  - Terraform remote state uses S3 backend + Dynamo-style lock (consensus locker) or consul for on-prem.
  - Secrets are stored in Vault HSM/KMS; small manual step needed to rotate/re-bind if keys change.
  - We assume offsite snapshot retention exists (daily) and last good snapshot id is known before an outage.

Quick glossary:
  - chassis: the collection of control-plane components (api, console, auth, db).
  - nodepool: GPU inference nodes.
  - kv-cache: local/redis-like ephemeral caches used for kv-prefix caching.

High-level choreography (phases)
1) Detection & Triage (T+0)
   - Alert triggers: control-plane DB corruption, lost control-plane quorum, or operator-initiated DR test.
   - Initial action: create incident channel (#dr-ops), set priority.
   - Identify last known-good snapshot id (e.g. s-2024-06-09-03).

2) Containment (T+10m)
   - Isolate affected clusters (prevent automated upgrades / autoscaler actions).
   - For cloud-hosted private control plane: disable external load-balancers to avoid split-brain.
   - If terraform CI is active, pause any apply pipelines (CI flag = DR_MODE).

3) Snapshot retrieval & verification (T+30m)
   - Pull snapshot manifest from offsite: aws s3 cp s3://redwood-backups/private/<deployment>/<snapshot>.tar.gz /tmp/restore/
   - Verify checksum: sha256sum <file> and compare to manifest.
   - Quick file-level verify: tar -tzf <file> | head -n 20  (ensure expected buckets/keys present)
   - NOTE: If checksum mismatch -> escalate to storage team and pick previous snapshot.

4) Terraform state & infra reconstruction (T+45m -> T+2h)
   - Rationale: we must avoid mismatched infra assumptions. Approach: Quiesce, then recreate minimal infra before restoring DBs.
   - Steps (operator):
     a) Export current terraform state (if reachable): terraform state pull > state-before-dr-$(date +%s).json
     b) If state backend unreachable, prepare a synthetic state file using last-known-ids from snapshot manifest (manual mapping).
     c) Set DR-tagged workspace: terraform workspace new dr-restore || terraform workspace select dr-restore
     d) Update backend config to use a *dedicated* recovery bucket to avoid clobbering production remote state (backend_override.tf or -backend-config).
     e) Run `terraform plan -var-file=dr-vars.hcl -target=module.private_network -target=module.control_plane_minimal` to bring up networking and control-plane load balancers only.
   - Hooks: we added terraform lifecycle hooks (pre-apply and post-apply) in modules:
     - pre-apply: validate-lock.sh -> checks for CI paused flag and state lock presence.
     - post-apply: register-backup-endpoint.sh -> updates offsite manifest with new access URL.

5) Data restore (DB + artifacts) (T+2h -> T+6h)
   - DB restore steps (Postgres example):
     - Stop writes to target DB (ensure replicas read-only).
     - Move current DB data dir to data-dir.bak.$TS (if local).
     - Restore: pg_restore --clean --if-exists -d redwood_control /tmp/restore/control-db.dump
     - Recreate replication slots and users using snapshot metadata (script: restore-users.sh).
   - Object-store: restore buckets and set lifecycle tags. Use `aws s3 sync` or `mc mirror` for MinIO.
   - Vault/secrets: unwrap wrapped key with HSM (operator step), rebind Vault namespaces to the restored control-plane cluster.

6) Service bootstrap & KV cache resync (T+6h -> T+8h)
   - Start critical services one-by-one: auth -> db -> api -> console -> schedulers -> node registration controller.
   - Avoid allowing inference nodes to pull large models immediately: set global traffic limit to 0 or pause nodepool autoscale.
   - Clear in-memory caches that could have stale pointers (redis-flushall across dedicated cache cluster).
   - Re-populate KV prefix caches from snapshot manifest via bulk import script if applicable.

7) Smoke checks and validation (T+8h -> T+10h)
   - Smoke checklist (fast automated):
     - curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer <ops-token>" https://controlplane.example.com/health | jq .status == \"ok\"
     - Run end-to-end sample inference with small model: POST /v1/generate -> expect 200 and latency < 800ms (internal SLO).
     - Validate model catalog entries and checksums match expectations.
     - Run small subset of N automated evals (5 prompts) and compare scores -> threshold: no more than 5% drift vs snapshot baseline.
   - Manual checks: console login, RBAC spot check, billing/usage counters plausible.

8) Failover completion & clean-up (T+10h -> T+12h)
   - Promote DR workspace to production (operator decision).
   - If promoted, migrate terraform state back to prod backend carefully: terraform state push OR use state mv operations.
   - Tear down temporary resources (dr-standby infra) after a successful 24h observation window.

Terraform-specific notes and pitfalls observed in dry-run:
  - Backend lock semantics differ across on-prem setups. We added a pre-apply guard that will fail fast when the locker is unreachable rather than risking split-state.
  - Terraform providers may attempt to recreate resources with same names but different IDs; always prefer `terraform import` for critical resources (LBs, DNS entries) instead of re-creating.
  - When restoring state from a snapshot manifest, keep a read-only copy of the snapshot manifest under version control in the recovery bucket.
  - Use `-parallelism=1` for critical restores where ordering matters (certs, DNS).

Example operator commands (cheat sheet):
  # set DR mode to pause automated CI applies
  curl -X POST https://internal-ci.redwood.local/api/flags -d '{"DR_MODE":true}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <ci-token>'

  # workspace and backend override
  terraform workspace new dr-restore || terraform workspace select dr-restore
  terraform init -backend-config="bucket=redwood-dr-state" -backend-config="key=staging/dr-restore.tfstate"
  terraform plan -var-file=dr-vars.hcl -target=module.control_plane_minimal -out dr-plan.out
  terraform apply dr-plan.out

  # pulling snapshot and verifying
  aws s3 cp s3://redwood-offsite/private/example-deploy/s-2024-06-09-03.tar.gz /tmp/restore/
  sha256sum /tmp/restore/s-2024-06-09-03.tar.gz
  tar -xzvf /tmp/restore/s-2024-06-09-03.tar.gz -C /tmp/restore/extracted/

Dry-run log (notes-to-self):
  - 2024-05-28 09:15: Ran terraform init with backend override; pre-apply guard prevented apply because locker endpoint returned 500. Good failure mode.
  - 2024-05-28 10:02 Imported control-plane LB (dns: cp-staging.example) with terraform import to avoid DNS swap. Record: lb-attach-20240528.txt
  - 2024-05-28 11:20 Snapshot manifest had missing user-role mapping for tenant-id 87; patched restore-users.sh to accept fallback_role.
  - 2024-05-28 13:45 Vault unwrap required operator HSM access; procedure added to on-call checklist.

Rollback and upgrade considerations (during/after DR)
  - If an upgrade was in progress at T-0: prefer rolling back control-plane to prior known-good version stored in artifacts bucket. Do not attempt a forward upgrade until 24h observation.
  - Keep model-serving runtime versions frozen while control-plane is in transitional state (mismatch in API contracts causes node rejections).
  - Document a fast rollback path: redeploy previous helm/chart artifact (artifact id in snapshot manifest) and run post-rollback smoke tests.

Post-restore playbook items to harden (action items):
  - Add a terraform `restore-state` helper that consumes snapshot manifest and generates a preliminary state pull file (PR #412).
  - Improve manifest format to list important resource IDs (LB, DNS, cert thumbprints, vault-keys).
  - Create a `dr-sanity` pipeline that runs automated smoke checks against a DR endpoint we stand up in dry-run mode.
  - Add automated checksum and manifest publishing to offsite snapshot pipeline (fail if missing fields).

Operator checklist (TL;DR)
  - [ ] Announce incident and set DR_MODE in CI
  - [ ] Fetch snapshot and verify checksum
  - [ ] Create dr-restore workspace and init with backend override
  - [ ] Apply minimal infra (network + control-plane LB)
  - [ ] Restore DBs and object-store buckets
  - [ ] Rebind Vault keys / secrets
  - [ ] Start services gradually, run smoke checks
  - [ ] Decide promote vs rollback and migrate terraform state accordingly

Open questions / unresolved:
  - What is the expected RTO for air-gapped on-prem customers with limited bandwidth? (need SLA mapping)
  - Should we automate vault key rewrap with a customer-provided HSM token exchange? (security review needed)
  - How to safely handle cross-account DNS updates if customer uses provider-managed DNS?

Appendix: small terraform snippet (for reference only - included in repo under examples/dr-hooks.tf)
  # module for minimal infra used during DR
  module "control_plane_minimal" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//control-plane?ref=dr-hooks-v1"
    network_id = var.network_id
    public_lb_allowed_cidrs = [var.ops_cidr]
    lifecycle = { prevent_destroy = true }
  }

Final notes:
  - This is intentionally concise and prescriptive — keep playbook steps small and scriptable.
  - Next steps: convert this doc into a runnable checklist in runbook-engine (runbook-id: rr-dr-2024-06) and add automation for steps that are purely mechanical (snapshot pull, checksum, minimal apply).

Notes to self: keep the language simple, avoid magic. If any step is >10 manual keystrokes, script it.
